title: Developing an OMOP-Standardized Prostate Cancer Database and Improving Data Quality Using NLP and PSA-Based Algorithms
authors: Wang, J.; Jackson, J. C.; Garza, A.; Nalla, S.; Ninnemann, T.; Zhang, Y.; Kuo, Y.-F.
abstract: ObjectiveTo develop and evaluate an Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership-(OMOP-) standardized prostate cancer database from the University of Texas Medical Branch (UTMB) Epic Electronic Health Record (EHR) and improve data quality using natural language processing(NLP) and prostate-specific antigen-(PSA) based algorithms. Materials and MethodsWe built a data pipeline to transform UTMB Epic EHR data for patients identified through the Galveston Cancer Registry (2010-2021) into OMOP Common Data Model (CDM) v5.4. Data quality was assessed by comparing the OMOP-standardized data with Galveston Cancer Registry data using availability agreement, Cohens kappa and Intraclass Correlation Coefficient. NLP was used to extract PSA, Gleason score, and cancer stage from clinical text, and PSA-based algorithms were used to identify missing treatment and biochemical recurrence. ResultsWe extracted 815 analytic cases from UTMB EHR. Among them, 700 (85.9%) were complete and concordant with the cancer registry. PSA showed excellent value agreement. Structured Gleason score and stage data were sparse (n<20), but NLP greately improved capture. Treatment agreement was good compared with the cancer registry and improved slightly for radical prostatectomy after applying a PSA-based algorithm. Using PSA trajectories, we identified 60 cases of biochemical recurrence. DiscussionThe OMOP-standardized data from UTMB showed good agreement with the cancer registry. However, structured EHR fields incompletely captured diagnosis, pathology, and treatment details. NLP and PSA-based algorithms substantially improved data capture. Manual review also revealed errors in registry data, showing that OMOP-standardized EHR data can complement and help improve cancer registry quality. Conclusion: OMOP standardization combined with NLP and PSA-based algorithms improved prostate cancer data quality and research readiness. Lay SummaryElectronic health record (EHR) systems contain valuable long-term health information about cancer, but their use is limited by difficulties in data extraction, the lack of standard data formats, and missing information in structured fields. In this study, we built a data pipeline to convert EHR data into the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model, a widely used standard format that facilitates data sharing and collaborative research. To address missing data, we used natural language processing (NLP, a computational technique that enables computers to interpret human language) to extract prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels, Gleason scores (a measure of cancer aggressiveness), and cancer stages from unstructured clinical notes. We also applied algorithms that track PSA blood trends over time to identify unrecorded cancer treatments and detect cancer recurrence. Comparing this database with a cancer registry demonstrated that standardized EHR records provide accurate clinical information and long-term follow-up. While structured EHR fields lacked key tumor characteristics, NLP dramatically improved their capture. Tracking PSA trends identified previously unrecorded treatments and flagged 60 potential cancer recurrences. Overall, combining standardized EHR formats with NLP and PSA-based algorithms creates a rich database to support real-world prostate cancer research.

infographic.key_insight: Standardizing prostate cancer EHR data to OMOP, then adding NLP and PSA-based rules, markedly improved capture of diagnosis, pathology, treatment, and recurrence information.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could make real-world prostate cancer data more complete and research-ready, while also helping identify missing or inconsistent registry records.
method: Built an OMOP CDM v5.4 pipeline from UTMB Epic EHR data for registry-identified prostate cancer cases (2010–2021).
Compared OMOP data quality with cancer registry records using agreement metrics.
Applied NLP to extract PSA, Gleason score, and stage from clinical text, plus PSA-based algorithms for missing treatment and biochemical recurrence.
infographic.evidence_signal: From 815 analytic cases, 700 (85.9%) were complete and concordant with the cancer registry; PSA agreement was excellent, and NLP substantially improved sparse Gleason/stage capture.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on local EHR structure, text quality, and PSA data availability, so the workflow may need site-specific validation before broader use.
infographic.paper_title: Developing an OMOP-Standardized Prostate Cancer Database and Improving Data Quality Using NLP and PSA-Based Algorithms

title: From examinations to consultations: a physician-reviewed Japanese benchmark for large language models in traditional Kampo medicine
authors: Takata, H.; Harada, Y.; Inoue, H.; Uneda, K.; Yoshino, T.; Nogami, T.
abstract: ObjectivesPatients and clinicians increasingly ask large language models (LLMs) about Kampo, Japans traditional medicine. Yet evaluations of LLMs have measured accuracy on examination questions, which ask what a model knows; a consultation asks whether it can apply that knowledge to the patient at hand. No benchmark had measured that. Materials and MethodsKampoBench comprises 74 consultation scenarios and 310 conversation-specific rubric criteria, following the design of HealthBench. Scenarios, criteria and reference answers were drafted by an LLM and revised by board-certified Kampo physicians. Ten current models from three vendors were evaluated. Because LLM graders are known to favor their own family, each response was graded by a model from each vendor. ResultsThe best model reached 74.8-86.3% across graders, the physician-revised reference answers 87.9-92.4%. Rankings were stable across graders (Spearmans rho 0.952-0.976), and the family-favoring deviation was 0.4 to 0.6 percentage points, below the bootstrap standard deviation of one measurement; grader leniency varied by 14.3 points. Models were most reliable on criteria about advising that care be sought (83.6%) and least reliable on those requiring a known crude-drug risk to be tied to the case (17.5%), though 79.2% of those responses named the drug. DiscussionThe shortfall lay in applying knowledge to the case rather than in holding it -- a distinction examination-format evaluations cannot make. ConclusionEvaluation in traditional medicine should measure the judgments a consultation requires, not recall alone. Quoted alongside the grader that produced it, a KampoBench score is a usable measure of those judgments. Lay summaryPeople increasingly ask artificial intelligence chatbots about Kampo, the traditional herbal medicine used alongside conventional care in Japan. Earlier tests used examination questions, which check what a chatbot knows. A real consultation asks something harder: whether the chatbot can apply that knowledge to the person asking. We built KampoBench, 74 realistic consultations in Japanese. For each one, specialist Kampo physicians reviewed a list of what a good answer should and should not contain, 310 items in all. We then tested ten current chatbots from three companies. The answers were scored by chatbots, and a chatbot might favor its own companys chatbots, so every answer was scored by one chatbot from each company. No such favoritism was detected, but the scorers differed in strictness. The best chatbot scored 75-86%, depending on the scorer; answers revised by physicians scored 88-92%. The chatbots were good at telling people to seek medical care. They were poor at relating a known risk of an herbal ingredient to the persons situation, such as noticing that two medicines the person already takes contain the same ingredient, often even when they named it. Tests of chatbots in traditional medicine should measure such judgments, not knowledge alone.

infographic.key_insight: KampoBench shifts LLM evaluation from memorizing Kampo facts to judging whether a model can apply them appropriately in patient-specific consultations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For traditional medicine use in real-world care, the study suggests consultation-style assessment is more informative than exam-style accuracy alone.
method: Built 74 Japanese Kampo consultation scenarios with 310 rubric criteria
LLM-generated drafts were revised by board-certified Kampo physicians
Ten current models from three vendors were scored, with each response graded by models from all vendors
infographic.evidence_signal: The top model scored 74.8–86.3% across graders, while physician-revised reference answers scored 87.9–92.4%; grader rankings were highly consistent (Spearman’s rho 0.952–0.976).
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on grader choice and vendor-specific leniency, so scores should be interpreted as benchmark performance rather than direct evidence of clinical safety or patient benefit.
infographic.paper_title: From examinations to consultations: a physician-reviewed Japanese benchmark for large language models in traditional Kampo medicine

title: Decision models can offload structured clinical tasks from large language models
authors: Ariel, D.; Laban, G.; Endelman, S.; Balicer, R.; Dagan, N.; Cohen, S.
abstract: Decision models like Jev read text and return probabilities, categories, or ordinal levels, with confidence scores for the latter two, at a fraction of large language models (LLMs) cost. We explored how Jev could be integrated into clinical workflows for all these output types: mortality risk estimation, categorical Choosing-Wisely decisions for patient questions, and ordinal colon cancer staging. With standard LLM-style inputs, Jev trailed five flagship LLMs: mortality AUROC was 0.822 versus 0.837-0.846; Choosing-Wisely accuracy, 87.7% versus 98.4-100%; and staging accuracy, 45.4% versus 94.2-100%. Developer-recommended input alterations improved staging accuracy to 75.8% with medical context, 82.1% with task decomposition, and 85.8% with both. None of Jevs staging errors had full confidence. Using Jev for fully confident staging decisions and LLMs for the rest was non-inferior to each LLM alone and cut flagship LLM costs by 33-44%. Prompted as designed, decision models may efficiently share structured clinical tasks with LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Decision models can take on structured clinical tasks, but they need task-specific prompting and may work best as a hybrid with LLMs.
infographic.clinical_relevance: In clinical NLP workflows, using a cheaper decision model for high-confidence cases and an LLM for the rest could reduce cost while preserving performance.
method: Compared Jev against five flagship LLMs on mortality risk, Choosing-Wisely categorization, and colon cancer staging.
Tested standard LLM-style prompting versus developer-recommended input changes, including medical context and task decomposition.
Evaluated a hybrid strategy that routed fully confident staging predictions to Jev and the remaining cases to LLMs.
infographic.evidence_signal: With standard prompting, Jev underperformed LLMs, but improved staging accuracy from 45.4% to 85.8% with both input changes, and the hybrid approach cut flagship LLM costs by 33-44% while remaining non-inferior.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depended strongly on prompt design, and staging errors were more common when Jev was not fully confident, so workflow integration needs careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: Decision models can offload structured clinical tasks from large language models

title: Diagnostic accuracy and clinician-rated reasoning quality dissociate in a blinded evaluation of large language models in psychiatry
authors: Jin, K. W.; Rostam-Abadi, Y.; Chaudhary, P.; Garrett, M. A.; Huang, A. S.; Montelongo, M.; Nagpal, C.; Shei, J.; Weathers, J.; Zhang, J. S.; Sharma, M. S.; Chen, Q.; Kim, J.; Malgaroli, M.; Mathis, W. S.; Rodriguez, C. I.; Selek, S.; Pittenger, C.; Yip, S. W.; Zaboski, B. A.; Xu, H.
abstract: BackgroundEvaluations of large language models (LLMs) in medicine rest largely on diagnostic accuracy. We report what we learned evaluating four frontier LLMs on psychiatric diagnosis, where we asked whether clinician assessment of model reasoning adds information that accuracy does not. MethodsFour LLMs produced ranked five-diagnosis differentials for 196 psychiatric vignettes (135 screened published case reports; 61 unpublished, clinician-authored). An automated adjudicator scored accuracy. On a random 30-vignette subset, five psychiatrists blinded to model identity judged correctness and rated reasoning on a 0-4 rubric adapted from the ACGME Psychiatry Milestones. We validated the adjudicator against the clinicians, measured the reproducibility of accuracy across generation runs and repeated adjudication, and tested whether computable reasoning trace features could substitute for clinician ratings. ResultsOn all 196 vignettes, automated top-5 accuracy ranged from 0.759 to 0.837, and the majority verdict of three adjudication passes separated one of six model pairs. On the 30 rated vignettes, clinician-determined accuracy separated no pair, while reasoning separated five. Two systems were equally accurate (0.827 each; difference bounded within {+/-}0.059, or {+/-}0.10 after Holm adjustment) yet differed by 0.70 reasoning points (95% CI, 0.50 to 0.90). The adjudicator agreed with held-out clinician majorities less closely than individual clinicians did (0.83 to 0.85 vs 0.89 to 0.96), regeneration changed top-1 correctness for 18 of 119 pairs, and reference strings that combined several diagnoses were scored as misses until split. Trace features that tracked ratings across model averages did not track them across individual traces. ConclusionsAccuracy did not distinguish models that clinicians rated differently, and automated accuracy depended on how it was scored. Where LLMs are meant to support clinical reasoning, structured clinician assessment of reasoning belongs in pre-deployment evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: Diagnostic accuracy alone missed important differences between large language models in psychiatry; clinician-rated reasoning quality separated models that looked equally accurate.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If LLMs are used to support clinical decision-making, evaluation should assess not just whether they are right, but how well they reason and explain their answers.
method: Four frontier LLMs generated ranked top-5 psychiatric differentials for 196 vignettes.
Automated adjudication scored accuracy across all cases; five psychiatrists blindly rated accuracy and reasoning on a 30-vignette subset.
The study compared automated scores, clinician judgments, run-to-run reproducibility, and computable trace features.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 196 vignettes, automated top-5 accuracy ranged from 0.759 to 0.837, while on the 30 clinician-rated cases, accuracy separated no model pair but reasoning separated five.
infographic.watch_item: Automated scoring and trace-based proxies may not capture clinically meaningful reasoning, so deployment evaluations should include blinded expert review.
infographic.paper_title: Diagnostic accuracy and clinician-rated reasoning quality dissociate in a blinded evaluation of large language models in psychiatry

title: AI chatbots abandon sleep apnoea referral when simulated patients minimise symptoms
authors: Ratneswaran, D.; Poirier, S.; Hamman, D.; Rykov, M.; Steier, J.
abstract: BackgroundPatients increasingly consult free artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots about their symptoms, but these models may favour agreement with the patient over accuracy. In obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), where most cases in the general population remain undiagnosed and diagnosis depends on referral, this could validate symptom denial. We tested whether consumer chatbots maintain guideline-concordant referral when a simulated patient minimises symptoms. MethodsSeven guideline-concordant and standardised OSA vignettes (apnoea-hypopnoea-index, AHI 8-52 events/h; body mass index 28-42 kg/m2) were presented to five free chatbots (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek V4 Flash and Grok-4.3) under neutral and symptom-minimising conditions (10 simulated conversations per model- vignette-condition cell; N=700). Referral maintenance was scored by a structured rubric and every capitulation was human-confirmed. ResultsAll chatbots maintained referral recommendations in neutral conversations (350/350; 100%). When simulated patients minimised symptoms and resisted referral, maintenance fell to 64.3% (225/350), a reduction of 35.7 percentage points (95% CI 5.5- 66.0; p=0.028). Rates ranged from 55.7% to 85.7% across chatbots, but evidence of between-chatbot differences was inconsistent across analyses. Rates differed across clinical vignettes (p=0.001). A variance analysis estimated greater variation between vignettes than between chatbots. In the three driving-risk vignettes, referral recommendations were abandoned in 46- 68% of symptom-minimising conversations, pooling all five chatbots within each vignette. ConclusionsConsumer AI chatbots abandoned correct OSA referral recommendations in about one-third of symptom-minimising conversations, with higher observed abandonment in simulated cases involving driving risk. This may delay appropriate assessment and raises patient- and public-safety concerns.

infographic.key_insight: When simulated patients downplayed obstructive sleep apnoea symptoms, consumer AI chatbots were much more likely to drop guideline-concordant referral advice.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This matters because a chatbot’s tendency to agree with symptom minimisation could contribute to delayed diagnosis and missed sleep apnoea referrals, especially in higher-risk cases such as driving risk.
method: Seven standardised OSA vignettes were tested across five free chatbots under neutral and symptom-minimising conditions.
Each model-vignette-condition cell used 10 simulated conversations, for a total of 700 conversations.
Referral maintenance was scored with a structured rubric and all capitulations were human-confirmed.
infographic.evidence_signal: Referral maintenance was 100% in neutral conversations but fell to 64.3% under symptom-minimising prompts, with larger drops in some vignettes and particularly in driving-risk scenarios.
infographic.watch_item: This was a simulated-conversation study, so real-world patient behavior, safety controls, and chatbot outputs in live clinical use may differ from the tested setup.
infographic.paper_title: AI chatbots abandon sleep apnoea referral when simulated patients minimise symptoms

title: ClinStigma: A Clinician-Guided Framework for Developing Synthetic Benchmarks of Contextual Stigmatizing Language in Clinical Documentation
authors: Izzo, J. A.; McIntyre, A. M.; Nguyen, J.; Bashaw, D.; Torrance, C. A.; Foster, J.
abstract: ObjectiveLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate, summarize, and evaluate clinical documentation, yet standardized methods for evaluating nuanced, context-dependent clinical language remain limited. Existing approaches rely primarily on annotated clinical corpora or keyword-based methods, restricting reproducibility, public dissemination, and systematic comparison across models. We present ClinStigma, a clinician-guided framework for constructing, annotating, and evaluating synthetic benchmarks of contextual stigmatizing language, demonstrated through ClinStigma-SUD, its inaugural implementation for substance use disorder documentation. Materials and MethodsCandidate clinical sentences were generated using a frontier language model and iteratively reviewed according to a clinician-developed annotation rubric refined through expert review in stigmatizing language. The resulting benchmark intentionally incorporates explicit stigmatizing, neutral, and contextually ambiguous ("gray-zone") documentation requiring clinical reasoning rather than keyword recognition. Three locally deployed open-weight LLMs were evaluated using zero-shot inference, followed by external evaluation using independently annotated clinical documentation from MIMIC-IV. ResultsClinStigma-SUD consists of 500 clinician-adjudicated synthetic clinical documentation sentences. Inter-rater agreement was 98.8% across the full benchmark (Cohens {kappa} = 0.976) and 94.0% within the intentionally ambiguous subset ({kappa} = 0.880). Under zero-shot prompting, binary accuracy ranged from 84.8% to 91.8% across evaluated models, while F1 for the ambiguous (gray) class ranged from 0.038 to 0.423. Zero-shot external evaluation on 3,716 annotated examples from the independently annotated Harrigian MIMIC-IV corpus yielded 84.4% accuracy (84.4% balanced accuracy; macro F1 0.824), against a 69.9% majority-class baseline. Stigmatizing-class F1 was 0.879 in the substance-related subgroup and 0.883 in the full external corpus. Discussion and ConclusionClinStigma establishes a reproducible clinician-guided framework for developing synthetic evaluation benchmarks for contextual clinical language. By combining structured clinical expertise, explicit annotation guidance, synthetic benchmark generation, and external evaluation, the framework enables open, privacy-preserving evaluation of language models while providing a scalable foundation for benchmark development across additional clinical specialties, including obstetrics, emergency medicine, and mental health.

infographic.key_insight: ClinStigma provides a clinician-guided way to build synthetic benchmarks that test whether models can recognize stigmatizing language in clinical notes, including hard gray-zone cases.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This could help developers and hospitals evaluate clinical NLP systems more safely and consistently before use in real documentation workflows.
method: Generated candidate clinical sentences with a frontier LLM.
Clinicians iteratively reviewed and refined an annotation rubric for stigmatizing, neutral, and ambiguous language.
Evaluated three open-weight LLMs with zero-shot prompts and tested external generalization on annotated MIMIC-IV documentation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The benchmark included 500 clinician-adjudicated sentences with very high agreement (kappa 0.976 overall), and external testing on 3,716 MIMIC-IV examples achieved 84.4% accuracy and 0.824 macro F1.
infographic.watch_item: Because the benchmark is synthetic and the ambiguous class remained difficult for models, performance may not fully reflect real-world clinical documentation complexity.
infographic.paper_title: ClinStigma: A Clinician-Guided Framework for Developing Synthetic Benchmarks of Contextual Stigmatizing Language in Clinical Documentation

title: A Zero-Shot Decision Model (Jev) Matches a Trained Classifier but Ranks Its Own Errors Worse: Calibrated, Split-Conformal Next-Procedure Recommendation in General Dentistry
authors: Rodrigues, C. C.; Rebello, S. D.
abstract: On real-world dental records, procedure history predicts the next procedure category well, and a simple history-aware classical model beats every large-language-model (LLM) design we tested. We study the question that follows every dental diagnosis: given a patients chart and most recent procedure, what should the dentist do next? Commercial dental artificial intelligence in 2026 is overwhelmingly diagnostic, and the closest published system for this sequencing task, MultiTP (Chen et al., 2024b), offers neither calibrated uncertainty, structured rationale, nor an evaluation as decision support. We introduce DentaCoPilot, a recommender that returns a calibrated top-K distribution over Current Dental Terminology (CDT) codes, a verbalised confidence label, an explicit abstain flag, and a chart-grounded rationale, and we compare four classical baselines with six LLM variants. On an apples-to-apples synthetic evaluation, classical baselines reach 0.567 top-1 while pure LLM variants trail at 0.267 to 0.467, and moving the backbone from Sonnet to Opus does not help. Prompt-conditioning a Sonnet LLM on the classical baselines candidate list closes most of the gap while preserving rationale and abstention; because the synthetic generator shares Markov structure with the bigram baseline, these synthetic rankings index pipeline behaviour, not externally valid clinical performance. We anchor external validity for the task on the public MEPS 2023 corpus (11,016 next-visit transitions across 5,088 patients): a history-aware model reaches 0.479 top-1 against 0.297 for a most-frequent baseline, is well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.031), and supports split-conformal selective prediction with a distribution-free coverage guarantee. A zero-shot LLM given only 1 this coarse history loses to the same classical baseline, so the LLMs value depends on rich charts rather than category history alone. Prospective clinician-in-the-loop validation and CDT-level real-data validation remain future work, contingent on clinical-data access and ethics approval that we have sought but not secured.

infographic.key_insight: A simple history-aware classical model outperformed several LLM approaches for predicting the next dental procedure, and adding calibrated uncertainty plus abstention made the system more decision-support ready.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For general dentistry workflows, next-step recommendations can be made more reliable by using chart history, confidence calibration, and selective abstention rather than relying on zero-shot LLM output alone.
method: Compared four classical baselines with six LLM variants for next-procedure recommendation.
Built DentaCoPilot to output top-K CDT codes, confidence labels, an abstain flag, and chart-grounded rationale.
Used split-conformal selective prediction to provide distribution-free coverage guarantees.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MEPS 2023 data (11,016 transitions from 5,088 patients), the history-aware model reached 0.479 top-1 accuracy versus 0.297 for a most-frequent baseline, with expected calibration error of 0.031.
infographic.watch_item: The stronger results come from retrospective and partly synthetic evaluation, so real-world CDT-level validation and prospective clinician testing are still needed.
infographic.paper_title: A Zero-Shot Decision Model (Jev) Matches a Trained Classifier but Ranks Its Own Errors Worse: Calibrated, Split-Conformal Next-Procedure Recommendation in General Dentistry

title: Deep Learning Trained Without Target-Domain Labels Improves Risk Stratification Over Expert Coronary Calcium Reading on Routine Attenuation Correction CT
authors: Shanbhag, A.; Miller, R. J.; Killekar, A.; Marcinkiewicz, A. M.; Zhou, J.; Lemley, M.; Kamagate, A.; Van Kriekinge, S. D.; Kavanagh, P. B.; Feher, A.; Miller, E. J.; Liang, J. X.; Berman, D. S.; Dey, D.; Leahy, R. M.; Slomka, P.
abstract: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) is an established measure of coronary atherosclerosis on computed tomography (CT). Many SPECT and most PET myocardial perfusion studies already include a low-dose CT scan from which coronary calcium could be reported, yet it almost never is. CAC may not be reported due to image noise, cardiac motion, or the absence of a reliable reference standard. Deep learning (DL) models trained on these low-dose CT scans inherit the same uncertainty, because their reference labels are drawn on the degraded images. We bypassed this limitation by training a DL CAC model entirely outside the target domain: expert labels from high-quality gated CT were inherited by synthetic ungated images derived from those same scans, so that no CTAC scan was annotated, and no real CTAC image was used, at any point in training. Models were trained using one center and externally tested in two other centers. Because each synthetic image is derived from the gated scan itself, expert gated segmentations remain valid voxel-for-voxel without registration. Using these pairs, we developed a cross-domain knowledge adaptation model (knowledge adaptation, KAD-CAC). The DL models were externally tested on 5969 patients with a median age of 64 (IQR 56 - 73), of whom 50.2% were male. The KAD-CAC model had higher Cohens kappa K (0.86, 95% CI 0.84 - 0.88) compared to a convolutional LSTM model (K 0.78, 95% CI 0.76 - 0.80, p<0.01), or models trained with only gated images (K 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 - 0.82, p<0.01). Net reclassification improvement for death or myocardial infarction over a clinical and perfusion baseline was greatest for the KAD-CAC model and exceeded that of expert CAC reading on the same CTAC scans (difference 0.089, 95% CI 0.051 to 0.125, p<0.001). A model trained without any labels from CTAC scans therefore stratified risk of death or MI better than expert reading of the same scans. Patients classified as CAC 0 by KAD-CAC had lower adjusted risk of death or MI than patients classified as CAC 0 by experts (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.25 - 0.98). We use paired synthetic ungated scans to transfer expert gated CAC annotations into the ungated domain, resulting in better vessel-level CAC scoring and improved risk reclassification compared with expert reading of the same scans. Automated CAC scoring could be added to every myocardial perfusion imaging report without additional imaging or radiation. The approach provides a general route to expert-quality supervision for any acquisition in which the native reference standard is unreliable.

infographic.key_insight: A coronary calcium deep-learning model trained without any target-domain CTAC labels, using synthetic ungated scans from gated CT, outperformed expert calcium reading for risk stratification.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could enable more reliable reporting of coronary artery calcium from routine attenuation-correction CT scans and improve identification of patients at risk for death or myocardial infarction.
method: Trained on expert-labeled high-quality gated CT, transferred to synthetic ungated images derived from the same scans.
Used cross-domain knowledge adaptation (KAD-CAC) without annotating or using real CTAC images during training.
Externally tested across two additional centers and compared with other DL models and expert reading.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 5,969 external patients, KAD-CAC showed higher agreement than comparator DL models and improved net reclassification for death or MI beyond clinical/perfusion baselines and expert CAC reading.
infographic.watch_item: Performance was evaluated retrospectively and may still depend on scanner, site, and workflow differences before real-world deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Learning Trained Without Target-Domain Labels Improves Risk Stratification Over Expert Coronary Calcium Reading on Routine Attenuation Correction CT

title: Ascending Aortic Calcium Identifies Patients at Risk Despite Normal Myocardial Flow, Perfusion and Coronary Calcium: A 13-Site Cohort Study
authors: Spielvogel, C.; Shanbhag, A.; Khanna, S.; Zuhair Kassem, T.; Lemley, M.; Yi, J.; Ramirez, G.; Kavanagh, P.; Kamagate, A.; Slipczuk, L.; Travin, M. I.; Buechel, R. R.; DeKemp, R. A.; Alexanderson, E.; Carvajal-Juarez, I.; Packard, R. R.; Al-Mallah, M.; Einstein, A. J.; Acampa, W.; Knight, S.; Le, V. T.; Mason, S.; Rosamond, T. L.; Miller, R. J.; Chareonthaitawee, P.; Dey, D.; Berman, D. S.; Di Carli, M. F.; Slomka, P.
abstract: BackgroundPatients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve (MFR) and no coronary artery calcium (CAC) on myocardial perfusion imaging are considered low risk. Yet, adverse events still occur and no routinely reported imaging marker stratifies residual risk. This study aims to determine whether fully automated ascending aortic calcification (AAC) from the attenuation correction CT stratifies risk in these patients. MethodsIn the multicenter REFINE-PET registry, AAC was quantified from non-contrast CT using deep learning aortic segmentation and Agatston scoring. Triple-normal was defined as stress total perfusion deficit (TPD) <5%, MFR >2 and CAC 0. The primary endpoint was cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission, with heart failure admission as key secondary endpoint. Cox models were adjusted for clinical confounders. ResultsOf 21,923 patients, 3,580 (16.3%) were triple-normal, of whom 1,322 (36.9%) had AAC (median Agatston 65, IQR 22-212). Agreement with three blinded readers was good to excellent (Intraclass correlation coefficient 0.87-0.90). Over a median follow-up of 52 months (IQR 26-69), 194 primary events occurred. Per standard deviation, AAC was independently associated with the primary endpoint (adjusted HR 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40; p<0.001), heart failure admission (adjusted HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.10-1.55; p=0.003) and all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.04-1.32; p=0.009). AAC improved model fit beyond clinical factors, MFR and TPD (p[≤]0.009), with modest gains in discrimination ({Delta}C 0.007-0.009). ConclusionsIn patients with normal PET readouts, automated AAC was independently associated with adverse outcomes, most strongly heart failure admission, beyond clinical risk factors, perfusion and flow. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIIn 3,580 patients with normal perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve and no coronary artery calcium on PET, more than one in three had ascending aortic calcification on the attenuation correction CT. C_LIO_LIAscending aortic calcification was independently associated with cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or heart failure admission (adjusted hazard ratio per SD 1.24, 95% CI 1.09-1.40), most strongly with heart failure admission. C_LIO_LIA fast, fully automated method scored ascending aortic calcification with agreement to expert readers similar to agreement between readers. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIA normal perfusion PET with normal flow and no coronary calcium does not mean uniformly low risk when the ascending aorta is calcified. C_LIO_LIBecause ascending aortic calcification is scored automatically from the CT acquired with every perfusion PET, it could be reported routinely without additional scanning, cost or radiation. C_LIO_LIPatients presumed low risk who have ascending aortic calcification may warrant heart failure-oriented prevention, such as natriuretic peptide screening, pending prospective validation. C_LI

infographic.key_insight: In patients with normal PET perfusion, normal myocardial flow reserve, and zero coronary calcium, ascending aortic calcium still identified a subgroup with higher residual cardiovascular risk.
infographic.clinical_relevance: A routinely available, fully automated measure from attenuation-correction CT may help refine risk stratification when standard PET readouts appear reassuring.
method: Multicenter REFINE-PET registry cohort of 21,923 patients; analysis focused on 3,580 triple-normal patients.
Ascending aortic calcification (AAC) was automatically segmented from non-contrast CT using deep learning and Agatston scoring.
Outcomes were assessed with adjusted Cox models for cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, heart failure admission, and all-cause mortality.
infographic.evidence_signal: AAC showed good agreement with blinded readers (ICC 0.87-0.90) and was independently associated with the primary endpoint (adjusted HR 1.24) with only modest discrimination gains beyond clinical and PET measures.
infographic.watch_item: The added predictive gain was modest, so AAC may be better viewed as a risk-refinement marker than a standalone decision tool until prospective implementation is validated.
infographic.paper_title: Ascending Aortic Calcium Identifies Patients at Risk Despite Normal Myocardial Flow, Perfusion and Coronary Calcium: A 13-Site Cohort Study

title: Language eligibility criteria and enrolled racial and ethnic composition in US clinical trials: a cross-sectional study
authors: Tolas, A.; Du, L. Y.; Schutz, N.; Schmiedmayer, P.; O'Sullivan, J. W.; Johnson, A.; Longenecker, C. K.; Sarraju, A.; Rodriguez, F.; Yang, E.; Kim, D. S.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Federal policy now requires sponsors to submit diversity action plans for clinical trials, yet the modifiable features of trial design associated with enrolled composition remain poorly characterized. English-language proficiency requirements are written into eligibility criteria and recorded as free text in a public registry, making them visible and, in principle, amenable to revision, but their relationship to enrolled composition has been examined only within single disease areas and in small samples of trials. We examined whether these requirements and documented language accommodation were associated with the racial and ethnic composition of enrolled participants. METHODS AND FINDINGS: We conducted a cross-sectional study of interventional trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov with at least one US site and posted results, using a registry snapshot retrieved in October 2026. The primary cohort comprised the 44,487 trials with exclusively US sites, of which 21,924 (49.3%) reported baseline race and 17,434 (39.2%) reported baseline ethnicity with counts that reconciled with the posted denominator. Both exposures were classified from free-text eligibility criteria using regular expressions validated against independent physician review of 150 trials. For the English-language requirement classifier, sensitivity was 88.2% and specificity was 99.2%. The outcome was the trial-level proportion of enrolled participants in each category, analyzed using generalized linear models adjusted for intervention class, therapeutic area, sponsor, phase, enrollment, sites, start year, US Census region, and the population composition of the trial's site states. An English-language proficiency requirement appeared in 5,736 trials (12.9%); its prevalence rose from 7.4% of trials starting in 2010 to 26.2% in 2023 (odds ratio [OR] per decade 2.91, P<0.001), whereas documented accommodation, an eligibility statement allowing participation in a language other than English (Spanish in 99.9% of flagged trials), remained rare (788 trials, 1.8%). The requirement was associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.77-0.93, P=0.001) and Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=0.85, 95% CI 0.79-0.91, P<0.001), with no evidence of an association for White participants (OR=0.99, 95% CI 0.95-1.04, P=0.75). Documented accommodation was associated with a higher proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants (OR=3.23, 95% CI 2.82-3.71, P<0.001). Geographic adjustment did not change the statistical significance of the requirement associations and attenuated the accommodation association. The main limitations were the cross-sectional design, which precludes causal inference; the restriction of enrollment analyses to trials reporting baseline demographics, which were more recent than those without such reporting; and possible misclassification of automatically classified exposures. CONCLUSIONS: English-language proficiency requirements became more than three times as common between 2010 and 2023 and were associated with lower enrolled proportions of Asian and Hispanic/Latinx participants. Less common documented language accommodation was associated with a higher enrolled proportion of Hispanic/Latinx participants. Because these criteria are investigator-written and publicly recorded, they may be a tractable target for improving enrollment equity, although whether revising them changes who enrolls requires prospective evaluation

infographic.key_insight: US clinical trials that require English proficiency enroll fewer Asian and Hispanic/Latinx participants, while language accommodation is uncommon.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Adding or removing language eligibility criteria is a modifiable trial-design feature that could affect who gets represented in clinical research.
method: Cross-sectional analysis of 44,487 interventional ClinicalTrials.gov trials with exclusively US sites and posted results.
Free-text eligibility criteria were classified for English-language requirements and language accommodation using validated regular expressions.
Adjusted generalized linear models tested associations with enrolled racial/ethnic composition and trial/site characteristics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The English-language requirement classifier was validated against physician review with 88.2% sensitivity and 99.2% specificity, and the study found the requirement in 12.9% of trials versus language accommodation in 1.8%.
infographic.watch_item: These are observational registry data, so the findings show association rather than proof that language criteria alone caused the enrollment differences.
infographic.paper_title: Language eligibility criteria and enrolled racial and ethnic composition in US clinical trials: a cross-sectional study

title: Multi-centre validation of MELD-graph for automated focal cortical dysplasia detection using 7T compared to paired 3T MRI
authors: Kronlage, C.; Ripart, M.; Piper, R. J.; Casella, C.; Klodowski, K.; Bauer, T.; Eriksson, M. H.; Bridgen, P.; Tisdall, M. M.; Bouschery, S. R.; Lange, A.; Pracht, E. D.; Stocker, T.; Cleary, J. O.; D'Arco, F.; Baldeweg, T.; Duncan, J. S.; Surges, R.; Ruber, T.; Rodgers, C. T.; Cope, T. E.; Carmichael, D. W.; O'Muircheartaigh, J.; Adler, S.; Wagstyl, K.
abstract: BackgroundSoftware tools can support MRI diagnosis of focal cortical dysplasias (FCDs) - subtle, surgically-treatable lesions that underlie drug-resistant focal epilepsy (DRFE). MELD-graph, a widely used open-source tool combining surface-based morphometry with a convolutional neural network, was developed using 1.5T and 3T MRI data. 7T MRI is increasingly used for lesion detection in DRFE. This study investigated whether MELD-graph is robust to domain shift at 7T. MethodsWe collated paired 3T and 7T T1-weighted MRI, and FLAIR where available, from 23 patients with FCD (6 histologically-verified, 17 identified radiologically) and 39 healthy controls at four epilepsy centres. Manual lesion labels were used as ground truth. MELD-graph was run on 3T images, on 7T images with the default pipeline, and on 7T images with adaptations for 7T MRI (SPM bias-field correction, SynthStrip skull-stripping, sub-millimetric FreeSurfer reconstruction), with and without ComBat harmonisation. FCD detection performance and surface morphometry features were compared. ResultsSensitivity for FCD detection was 65% (15/23) at 3T, 48% (11/23) for 7T default and 52% (12/23) for 7T adapted, with Combat harmonisation. Among radiologically 3T-negative patients, 2/8 were detected at 3T and 3/8 at 7T; and among histologically confirmed FCD, 3/6 at 3T and 1/6 at 7T. Specificity was significantly lower at 7T (default 39%, adapted 45%) than 3T (76%). False-positives predominantly occurred in the basal temporal lobes. ComBat harmonisation improved specificity in all conditions and largely compensated for field-strength dependent differences in surface morphometry features. Adding FLAIR at 7T increased false-positive predictions. ConclusionSensitivity is comparable but specificity of MELD-graph is lower at 7T compared to 3T. Adaptations for 7T MRI can reduce segmentation errors but do not significantly improve FCD detection, while harmonisation improves performance. The adapted pipeline is released open-source. 7T MELD-graph outputs may inform radiologist review in challenging cases but require cautious interpretation.

infographic.key_insight: MELD-graph kept similar sensitivity for focal cortical dysplasia at 7T MRI, but specificity dropped versus 3T, even after 7T-specific pipeline adjustments.
infographic.clinical_relevance: 7T outputs may help support radiologist review in difficult epilepsy cases, but false positives mean results should be interpreted cautiously rather than used alone.
method: Paired 3T and 7T MRI from 23 patients with FCD and 39 healthy controls across four epilepsy centres were analyzed.
MELD-graph was tested on 3T, on 7T with the default pipeline, and on 7T with adaptations for bias correction, skull-stripping, and sub-millimetric reconstruction.
ComBat harmonisation was also evaluated, with and without FLAIR at 7T.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation on paired multicentre data showed 65% sensitivity at 3T versus 48%-52% at 7T, while specificity fell from 76% at 3T to 39%-45% at 7T.
infographic.watch_item: The main implementation concern is a higher false-positive rate at 7T, especially in the basal temporal lobes, which could reduce clinical confidence if not carefully reviewed.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-centre validation of MELD-graph for automated focal cortical dysplasia detection using 7T compared to paired 3T MRI

title: Prospective validation of an uncertainty-aware machine learning model for secondary progressive multiple sclerosis classification
authors: Parakkal Sreenivasan, A.; Noui, Y.; Erngren, I.; Spjuth, O.; Burman, J.; Kultima, K.
abstract: BackgroundRelapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) often progresses to secondary-progressive MS (SPMS), but diagnosis is typically retrospective, delaying potential interventions. Existing rule-based and machine learning approaches often lack prospective validation and provide no uncertainty estimates, limiting clinical adoption. ObjectiveTo prospectively evaluate a conformal prediction (CP)-enabled random forest model for reproducing clinician-recorded disease course labels in the Swedish Multiple Sclerosis Registry (SMSReg) and compare its classifications with the Lorscheider criteria. MethodsThe CP model was trained and calibrated on SMSReg-2022 (10,787 individuals, 85,461 hospital visits) and then validated on SMSReg-2025 (15,719 individuals, 45,077 hospital visits; not included in the SMSReg-2022 training/calibration/testing datasets). Performance was assessed at the hospital visit and individual levels and compared with the Lorscheider criteria. ResultsThe model maintained good calibration on the prospective dataset. At the per-hospital visit-level, the model accuracies were 92% (RRMS) and 95% (SPMS). At the individual level, sensitivity was 98%, specificity 89%, and F1-score 0.75. With clinician-recorded labels as reference, the model showed higher sensitivity than the Lorscheider criteria (98% vs. 71%), more transition assignments (90% vs. 57%), and higher F1-score (0.76 vs. 0.69). ConclusionThe CP-enabled model prospectively reproduced clinician-recorded disease course labels with calibrated uncertainty, supporting harmonization and decision support.

infographic.key_insight: A conformal prediction-enabled random forest prospectively reproduced clinician-recorded MS disease course labels with calibrated uncertainty, including better SPMS-related performance than Lorscheider criteria.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This suggests a potentially useful decision-support approach for harmonizing secondary progressive multiple sclerosis classification in registry-based care.
method: Trained and calibrated on Swedish MS Registry 2022 data.
Prospectively validated on an independent 2025 registry cohort not used in training.
Compared predictions against clinician labels and the Lorscheider criteria at visit and patient levels.
infographic.evidence_signal: Prospective validation showed good calibration, with per-visit accuracies of 92% for RRMS and 95% for SPMS, and individual-level sensitivity of 98% and specificity of 89%.
infographic.watch_item: The model reproduces registry clinician labels rather than a definitive biological gold standard, so implementation depends on local data quality and workflow fit.
infographic.paper_title: Prospective validation of an uncertainty-aware machine learning model for secondary progressive multiple sclerosis classification

title: Mapping polygenic risk scores to brain cells: insights for neurodegenerative diseases
authors: Simmonds, E.; McKeever, A.; Yaman, U.; Leonenko, G.; Kimatova, K.; Taylor, P.; Chandran, S.; Ryten, M.; Khakh, B.; O'Brien, J. T.; Spires-Jones, T.; Salih, D. A.; Escott-Price, V.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) are driven by multiple related yet distinct pathological processes that evolve over decades, resulting in substantial clinical and neuropathological heterogeneity. Postmortem examinations of older individuals frequently reveal multiple coexisting neuropathologies, however, the underlying pathological processes cannot be easily assessed directly in living individuals. To quantify pathology-specific genetic signatures, we analysed a spectrum of NDDs using polygenic risk scores (PRSs) in the UK Biobank, restricting analyses to genes reported to be expressed in major brain cell-types, including microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and neurons. We found substantial overlap among purportedly cell-type specific gene sets (21-29%), with APOE or neighbouring genes from the APOE locus represented in all gene sets, indicating that current cell-type specific annotations capture considerable shared genetic variation across cell-types. Jointly, cell-type specific PRSs explained a large proportion (60-93%) of the genetic liability for NDDs in which dementia is a major clinical manifestation. Alzheimers disease (AD) showed associations across all cell-types, with oligodendrocyte- and astrocyte-based PRSs demonstrating strong effects independent of APOE. AD PRS and APOE status independently differentiated Parkinsons disease (PD) with dementia from PD without dementia. PD without dementia and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) exhibited distinct genetic profiles, with limited overlap with other NDDs. Collectively, these findings reveal both shared and disease-specific genetic contributions across neurodegenerative disorders and demonstrate that currently available cell-type specific gene sets capture substantial overlapping genetic risk. The imperfect alignment between clinical phenotypes and underlying pathology, coupled with the extensive overlap of gene expression across these cell types, underscores the persistent challenges in resolving the genetic architecture of neurodegenerative diseases and elucidating their underlying biological mechanisms.

infographic.key_insight: Polygenic risk scores built from brain cell-type gene sets capture substantial and partly shared genetic risk across neurodegenerative diseases, with Alzheimer’s showing the broadest cell-type associations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These results may help refine genetic stratification of neurodegenerative disease subtypes, especially dementia-related presentations, but they are not yet a standalone clinical tool.
method: Analyzed UK Biobank polygenic risk scores across multiple neurodegenerative diseases.
Restricted PRS construction to genes reported in microglia, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and neurons.
Compared cell-type-based scores and APOE effects across disease phenotypes and dementia status.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the abstract, cell-type-specific PRSs explained about 60–93% of genetic liability for neurodegenerative diseases where dementia is a major clinical feature, and the authors report 21–29% overlap among cell-type gene sets.
infographic.watch_item: Current cell-type annotations overlap substantially, so PRS signals may not cleanly map to distinct brain cell biology and should be interpreted cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Mapping polygenic risk scores to brain cells: insights for neurodegenerative diseases

title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study
authors: Di Lisio, F.; Soilleux, E. J.; Jaeckle, F.
abstract: BackgroundMachine Learning (ML) has shown promise in histopathological diagnosis, but rare tumours, like duodenal epithelial neoplasms, are challenging because large, labelled datasets are difficult to assemble. We propose a data-efficient ML pipeline for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia in whole-slide images. MethodsWe assembled a five-hospital dataset of haematoxylin and eosin-stained duodenal biopsy whole slide images (WSIs) at 10x magnification, comprising 8,027 normal and 401 neoplastic biopsies, including adenomas, carcinomas and neuroendocrine tumours. WSIs were divided into patches and encoded using the Hibou-B foundation model. We compared global standardisation with unsupervised site-specific standardisation of patch embeddings. Our pipeline combined principal component analysis, a Gaussian mixture model and a Random Forest classifier. We assessed generalisability using leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation across four hospitals and on an independent test set from a fifth hospital. ResultsIn leave-one-hospital-out cross-validation, the pipeline achieved a mean accuracy of 90%, sensitivity of 96%, specificity of 83% and an AUC of 0.96. On the external test hospital, it achieved 94% accuracy, 93% sensitivity, 95% specificity, and AUC of 0.97. Site-specific standardisation improved mean cross-validation accuracy by 20 percentage points compared with global standardisation, while the Gaussian mixture pipeline improved accuracy by 12 percentage points compared with mean pooling of patch embeddings. ConclusionsWe present a data-efficient ML approach for detecting duodenal epithelial neoplasia from WSIs. Strong performance was maintained across hospitals and on an independent external test cohort despite the limited number of neoplastic training cases, supporting the feasibility of foundation-model-based approaches for rare histopathological diagnoses.

infographic.key_insight: A foundation-model-based, data-efficient pipeline can detect duodenal epithelial neoplasia from whole-slide biopsy images with strong cross-hospital performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach could help support histopathology workflows for rare duodenal tumours, where labelled training data are scarce.
method: Used haematoxylin and eosin whole-slide images from 5 hospitals, split into patches and encoded with the Hibou-B foundation model.
Compared global standardisation with unsupervised site-specific standardisation of patch embeddings.
Applied PCA, Gaussian mixture modelling, and a Random Forest classifier for detection.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across leave-one-hospital-out validation, performance was 90% accuracy with AUC 0.96, and on an external hospital test set it reached 94% accuracy with AUC 0.97.
infographic.watch_item: Results are promising but need prospective validation and workflow testing before real-world deployment, especially given the small number of neoplastic cases.
infographic.paper_title: Data-efficient machine learning for the detection of duodenal neoplasia: a multi-centre study

title: Full stack academic publishing in seizures with artificial intelligence: a cautionary tale
authors: Kerr, W. T.; Pellinen, J.; McFarlane, K. N.; Goldenholz, D. M.
abstract: SignificanceThere is potential for generative artificial intelligence (AI) to perform "full stack" academic publishing, including comprehensive manuscript fabrication, "peer"-review, and editorial decision making. This study evaluated the benefits and cautions in using AI for full stack academic publishing in clinical research about seizures. MethodsThree epileptologists each selected 1 published manuscript in Epilepsia and produced an AI-fabricated manuscript about seizures. AI tools were then used to perform "peer"-review and make editorial decisions with minimal human supervision. The rates of identifying AI-fabricated manuscripts and editorial decisions among the epileptologists was analyzed, and epileptologists observations on how AI differed from typical human "peer"-review and editorial decisions was collected. ResultsFour of 6 (67%) pairs of AI-fabricated and human-generated manuscripts were correctly identified. Only 1 AI-fabricated manuscript was editorially rejected, whereas another had a subtle indicator of fabrication. When compared to human content, AI generated content was comprehensive, detailed, and based on the highest standard of academic publication. However, generated content was more verbose, used more structured responses, and more critical feedback. ConclusionsThese results demonstrate that the quality of AI-fabricated manuscripts about clinical research in seizures was sufficiently high that the current methods of peer and editorial review could not easily distinguish fabricated content compared to human-written content. Moreover, AI review and editorial decisions were high quality and appeared reasonable in many cases. AI tools have matured to the point that there should be thoughtful policies that permit AI assistance but prohibit insufficiently supervised autonomous scientific submissions, reviews, and editorial decisions. Highlights- The maturity of AI tools to assist in manuscript generation, peer-review, and editorial decisions comes with cautions. - Only 1 of 3 artificial intelligence (AI) fabricated manuscripts about seizures were reliably identified and rejected. - This study describes characteristics of AI-generated peer-review and editorial comments that had insufficient human oversight.

infographic.key_insight: AI can now produce seizure research manuscripts, peer reviews, and editorial decisions that often look convincing enough to challenge human detection.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This raises publication-governance concerns for medical research, suggesting AI can support drafting and review but should not be left to make unsupervised scientific decisions.
method: 3 epileptologists each created one AI-fabricated seizure manuscript based on a published Epilepsia paper.
AI tools were then used to simulate peer review and editorial decisions with minimal human oversight.
Researchers compared AI-fabricated vs human-written papers and recorded epileptologists’ ability to identify them.
infographic.evidence_signal: Epileptologists correctly identified 4 of 6 AI-fabricated vs human manuscript pairs (67%), and only 1 AI-fabricated manuscript was rejected by AI editorial review.
infographic.watch_item: A key concern is that AI-generated academic content may appear high-quality and authoritative while still being fabricated, so human oversight and policy guardrails are essential.
infographic.paper_title: Full stack academic publishing in seizures with artificial intelligence: a cautionary tale

title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification
authors: Rohani, F.; Mostafavi, S.; Ebrahimifakhar, P.; Zomorrodi, R.; Mueller, A.
abstract: BackgroundAttention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by persistent symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity that significantly affect cognitive, academic, and social functioning. Although electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a promising non-invasive tool for identifying objective neurophysiological biomarkers of ADHD because of its high temporal resolution and cost-effectiveness, many existing machine learning studies rely on single-domain EEG features, which may not adequately capture the complex functional organization of the brain. MethodsThis study proposes a subject-level EEG classification framework that integrates three complementary feature domains: spectral characteristics, weighted Phase Lag Index (wPLI)-based functional connectivity, and topological descriptors derived from persistent homology. EEG recordings from 121 subjects were preprocessed and segmented into overlapping windows for feature extraction. Window-level features were aggregated to generate subject-level representations. Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) was employed to select the 110 most informative features from an initial set of 1,043 descriptors. Five machine learning classifiers, including Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest, XGBoost, CatBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), were evaluated using stratified five-fold cross-validation. An ablation study was further conducted to assess the contribution of each feature domain. Model interpretability was investigated using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), two widely adopted Explainable Artificial Intelligence techniques for interpreting machine learning models. ResultsAmong the evaluated classifiers, the SVM achieved the highest classification performance, yielding an accuracy of 80.17%, an F1-score of 80.95%, a balanced accuracy of 80.14%, a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 86.72%, and a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 87.34%. The ablation study demonstrated that combining spectral, functional connectivity, and topological features consistently outperformed individual feature domains, highlighting the complementary nature of these representations. Explainable AI analyses further identified functional connectivity features as the primary contributors to classification performance while confirming the additional value of spectral and topological descriptors. ConclusionsThe proposed framework demonstrates that integrating spectral analysis, functional connectivity, and topological data analysis provides an effective and interpretable approach for subject-level ADHD classification from EEG recordings. The combination of recursive feature selection, multi-domain feature fusion, ablation analysis, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence establishes a transparent and reproducible pipeline that may facilitate the development of reliable EEG-based clinical decision-support systems for ADHD.

infographic.key_insight: A multi-domain EEG model combining spectral, connectivity, and topological features improved subject-level ADHD classification, with SVM performing best.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This work suggests EEG-based machine learning may help support more objective ADHD biomarker research, but it is not ready to replace clinical diagnosis.
method: EEG from 121 subjects was preprocessed and split into overlapping windows.
Features were extracted from three domains: spectral, wPLI-based functional connectivity, and persistent-homology topology.
RFE selected 110 features, and five classifiers were tested with stratified five-fold cross-validation plus ablation and SHAP/LIME interpretation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The best model was SVM, reaching 80.17% accuracy, 80.95% F1-score, 80.14% balanced accuracy, 86.72% ROC-AUC, and 87.34% PR-AUC.
infographic.watch_item: The dataset is relatively small, so performance may not generalize well without external validation on independent cohorts.
infographic.paper_title: A Multi-Domain EEG Framework Integrating Spectral, Functional Connectivity, and Topological Features for Subject-Level ADHD Classification

title: Microbial traits have minimal power for predicting death from bloodstream infection
authors: Gilliland, R.; Valdes-Tresanco, M. E.; Plakhotnyk, A.; Westlund, A.; Smith, J. T.; Pham, T. M.; Mortimer, T. D.; Walker, B. J.; Earl, A. M.; Grad, Y. H.; MacDonald, M. E.; Lewis, I. A.; PRIME Consortium,
abstract: Bloodstream infection (BSI) is a life-threatening condition where the risk of dying is affected by both patient-and pathogen-related factors. Certain microbial traits (e.g., virulence genes) are thought to affect survival rates from BSIs, but the magnitude of their impact on human mortality remains unclear. To address this, we analyzed the microbial genomes, quantitative proteomes, and electronic medical records (EMRs) from 35,746 BSIs from Calgary, Canada (2006-2022). We show that EMR-based machine learning models accurately predict 30-day mortality (AUC=0.83), but surprisingly, integrating >70,000 microbial genes/proteins does not improve this performance. We demonstrate that microbial factors co-segregate with specific patient cohorts and are therefore not independent predictors of risk. We conclude that microbial virulence factors have minimal impact on mortality rates from BSIs. One-Sentence SummaryMicrobial genes and protein abundance levels have minimal power for predicting 30-day mortality in bloodstream infections.

infographic.key_insight: Patient data in EMRs predicted 30-day bloodstream-infection mortality well, but adding large-scale microbial genes and proteins did not meaningfully improve prediction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: For risk stratification in bloodstream infection, host and clinical features appear far more useful than microbial trait profiling for estimating short-term mortality.
method: Analyzed 35,746 bloodstream infections from Calgary, Canada (2006–2022).
Combined microbial genomes, quantitative proteomes, and electronic medical record data.
Compared machine-learning mortality models with and without >70,000 microbial genes/proteins.
infographic.evidence_signal: EMR-based models achieved an AUC of 0.83 for 30-day mortality, and performance did not improve when microbial features were added.
infographic.watch_item: Microbial factors may cluster with specific patient cohorts, so associations can be confounded and should not be treated as independent predictors.
infographic.paper_title: Microbial traits have minimal power for predicting death from bloodstream infection

title: WHITE-Net : White matter HyperIntensities Tissue Extraction using deep learning Network
authors: Cathala, C.; Roduit, V.; Carneiro, F.; Heffernan, M.; Vanderbecq, Q.; Colliot, O.; Kherif, F.; Thiran, J.-P.; Bussy, A.; Draganski, B.
abstract: White matter hyperintensities (WMH) are a hallmark of cerebral small vessel disease, a highly prevalent condition in aging, making their accurate detection in large-scale magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies critically important. Currently available semi-automated and automated segmentation methods are frequently limited by sensitivity to variations in imaging conditions and computational constraints, restricting their applicability across diverse acquisition settings. We present WHITE-Net, a deep learning-based framework for automated WMH segmentation built on a 3D ResUNet architecture and trained on multisite MRI data encompassing substantial variability in scanner vendors, acquisition protocols, spatial resolution, and image characteristics. Evaluated across three independent datasets - BrainLaus, ADNI, and WMH Challenge, WHITE-Net achieves high segmentation accuracy and ranks among the top-performing methods across datasets, enabling a comprehensive assessment of generalizability in varied imaging environments. WHITE-Net maintains stable performance in a wide spectrum of lesion loads and demonstrates a favorable balance between precision and recall, effectively limiting false positive detections - a common limitation of existing approaches. Beyond accuracy, WHITE-Net requires no parameter tuning and offers fast inference times, making it well-suited for deployment in large-scale neuroimaging studies. The obtained results highlight the value of training on diverse multisite data for improving generalizability and position WHITE-Net as a reliable, scalable tool for automated WMH segmentation in computational anatomy research.

infographic.key_insight: WHITE-Net is a deep learning model that segments white matter hyperintensities accurately across diverse MRI settings by training on multisite, variable-quality data.
infographic.clinical_relevance: It could help large-scale neuroimaging studies quantify small vessel disease more reliably and efficiently without manual tuning.
method: 3D ResUNet-based segmentation model
Trained on multisite MRI data with varied scanners, protocols, and resolutions
Designed for fast inference and minimal parameter tuning
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was evaluated on three independent datasets (BrainLaus, ADNI, and WMH Challenge) and performed strongly across different lesion loads and imaging conditions.
infographic.watch_item: As with any automated segmentation tool, performance may vary on unseen acquisition settings or extreme image artifacts, so local validation is important.
infographic.paper_title: WHITE-Net : White matter HyperIntensities Tissue Extraction using deep learning Network

title: AI-Assisted Tissue-Based Antibody Interpretation in Autoimmune Encephalitis: Prospective Validation and Reader Study
authors: Cao, Z.; Xie, D.; Zou, S.; Li, D.; Martinez-Martinez, P.; Zong, S.; Zhang, Z.
abstract: Tissue-based assays provide broad screening for neural autoantibodies but remain vulnerable to technical and reader-dependent variability. We evaluated an integrated workflow combining automated 3,3'-diaminobenzidine tissue-based assay processing, digital whole-slide imaging, and interpretable deep learning. Model development used 2,357 retrospective serum and cerebrospinal fluid images referred from more than 80 institutions and processed in a centralized laboratory, with reference labels established by expert-consensus tissue-based assay interpretation. A prospective validation cohort included 200 images from 200 unique patients (154 positive and 46 negative; 100 serum and 100 cerebrospinal fluid). The same images were evaluated by two expert and two novice readers in a fixed-order two-round study, with unaided interpretation followed by artificial-intelligence-assisted interpretation after a washout of at least two weeks. The standalone binary classifier achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.922, accuracy of 86.5%, sensitivity of 85.7%, and specificity of 89.1% in prospective validation. Pooled reader accuracy was 90.4% in the unaided round and 97.4% in the artificial-intelligence-assisted round (McNemar P < 0.001), with specificity of 82.6% and 99.5%, respectively. Novice-reader accuracy was 83.3% unaided and 96.5% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001), approaching unaided expert accuracy of 97.5%. Among tissue-based-assay-positive cases, reader accuracy for cytoplasmic/nuclear antigen-associated versus neural surface antigen-associated staining-pattern subclassification was 88.8% unaided and 94.0% with artificial-intelligence assistance (P < 0.001). These findings support further multicentre, cross-platform evaluation of artificial-intelligence-assisted neural autoantibody tissue interpretation. Abbreviated summaryCao et al. report prospective validation of an automated tissue-based neural autoantibody workflow combining digital imaging and interpretable deep learning. Artificial-intelligence-assisted reading was associated with higher interpretation accuracy, particularly among less-experienced readers, supporting further multicentre validation across laboratories and imaging platforms.

infographic.key_insight: An interpretable deep-learning workflow for tissue-based neural autoantibody assays improved reader interpretation, especially for less-experienced readers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This approach may help standardize autoimmune encephalitis antibody screening by reducing reader-dependent variability in tissue-based assay interpretation.
method: Trained on 2,357 retrospective serum and CSF images from >80 institutions
Prospective validation on 200 unique patient images with expert-consensus reference labels
Two experts and two novices read cases unaided, then with AI assistance after a 2+ week washout
infographic.evidence_signal: In prospective validation, the standalone classifier reached AUC 0.922, and AI-assisted pooled reader accuracy rose from 90.4% to 97.4% with a large specificity gain.
infographic.watch_item: Results came from centralized-lab images and need broader multicentre, cross-platform validation before routine deployment.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Tissue-Based Antibody Interpretation in Autoimmune Encephalitis: Prospective Validation and Reader Study

title: Clinical utility of plasma APOE proteotyping for Alzheimer's disease risk and prognosis
authors: Shi, R.; Choity, L. T.; Farinas, M. F.; Zeng, X.; Emanuel, J. E.; Saeed, A.; Reis, S. E.; Lopez, O. L.; Kamboh, M. I.; Cohen, A. D.; Gildengers, A. G.; Wilckens, K. A.; Karikari, T. K.
abstract: BackgroundAlzheimers disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder strongly influenced by genetic factors, with apolipoprotein E (APOE) {varepsilon}4 allele being the most established risk variant. Although DNA-based genotyping remains standard, plasma proteotyping may provide scalable, isoform-specific alternatives. Here, we aimed to investigate the clinical utility of APOE proteotyping as a surrogate for genotyping in different clinical and research cohorts. MethodsPlasma APOE4 protein were quantified using the NULISAseq CNS panel across four cohorts (ADRC, HeartSCORE, LATTICE, and ALPS). DNA-based APOE genotyping was the reference standard. Proteotyping thresholds for APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status and copy number were derived in ADRC and externally validated in the other cohorts. Logistic, proportional-odds, and Cox proportional-hazards models compared genotype- and proteotype-defined groups in relation to amyloid positivity, cross-sectional CDR global scores, and time to CDR-SB worsening, respectively. ResultsPlasma APOE4 accurately classified APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status in ADRC (AUC=0.977, 95%CI 0.967-0.985; threshold 5.78 NULISA protein quantification [NPQ] value) and achieved near-perfect external validation in HeartSCORE, LATTICE, and ALPS (all AUCs=1.000, 95%CI 1.000-1.000). Plasma APOE4 also well-differentiated heterozygous from homozygous {varepsilon}4 carriers (ADRC AUC=0.879, 95%CI 0.834-0.921; threshold 12.23 NPQ value). Genotype- and proteotype-defined {varepsilon}4 carrier status showed similar associations with amyloid positivity (OR=4.40 vs 4.45), higher CDR global scores (OR=1.50 for both), and CDR-SB worsening (HR=1.22 for both). DiscussionPlasma APOE4 proteotyping accurately distinguished genotype-defined APOE {varepsilon}4 carrier status and copy number while demonstrating AD-related associations comparable to DNA genotyping.

infographic.key_insight: Plasma APOE4 proteotyping can closely match DNA APOE genotyping for identifying APOE ε4 carrier status and copy number, with similar Alzheimer’s disease associations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If validated broadly, this blood-based approach could offer a scalable alternative to genetic testing for risk stratification and prognosis in Alzheimer’s disease research and care settings.

infographic.paper_title: Clinical utility of plasma APOE proteotyping for Alzheimer's disease risk and prognosis
